sections.text:
Let no one be misled because the Apostle often omits the name of the Father and the Holy Spirit when mentioning baptism, or suppose from this that invocation of the names is unnecessary. “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ”; and again, “As many as were baptized into Christ were baptized into his death.”

For the name “Christ” is a confession of the whole mystery: it indicates God who anointed, the Son who was anointed, and the Spirit who is the anointing. We learned this from Peter in Acts concerning “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit”; and from Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he anointed me”; and from the Psalmist: “Therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”

Scripture also sometimes mentions only the Spirit in connection with baptism: “We were all baptized in one Spirit into one body”; “You will be baptized in the Holy Spirit”; and, “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.” Yet no one would therefore call a baptism complete in which only the name of the Spirit were invoked.

The tradition given in the life-giving grace must remain inviolate. The One who redeems our life from corruption gave us the power of renewal, whose beginning is faith and whose reality is held in mystery, bringing great salvation to souls. Therefore to add something or remove something from what was delivered is plainly to fall away from eternal life.

If in baptism the separation of the Spirit from the Father and Son is dangerous for the baptizer and useless to the recipient, how can it be safe for us to tear the Spirit away from Father and Son?

Faith and baptism are two modes of salvation flowing together and inseparable. Faith is perfected through baptism, baptism is founded upon faith, and both are completed by the same names. As we believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, so we are baptized into the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Confession goes before, introducing us into salvation; baptism follows, sealing our assent.

translator_notes: Basil reads the title 'Christ' trinitarily: the anointing involves God, the anointed Son, and the Spirit as anointing.
The chapter defends the integrity of the baptismal formula rather than a baptism invoking only one divine person.
